title: Serial Match: AP-Only Recovery for Exchange Buyers
one_liner: A success-fee audit that takes one accounts-payable export from an independent rotable pool or Part 145 station, finds money its repair vendors already owe, and collects it. It starts with credits the vendor has already conceded, then moves to repeat-failure claims.
customer: Independent rotable exchange pools, parts resellers and Part 145 stations that buy a few hundred outsourced repairs and exchange units a year from 10 or more shops, roughly $5-40M of repair spend (my assumption, unverified). The buyer is the Controller or VP Materials at a firm with a 2-4 person back office. These firms sit outside power-by-the-hour contracts, so the warranty exposure is theirs. They multi-source on price, so they have little vendor-relationship fear. They also see the same serial number pass through many hands. Regionals, EMS operators and lessors are phase 2.
problem: The parent idea had four named weaknesses: PBH and maintenance-plan contracts remove warranty exposure for many small fleets, integrating with each operator's maintenance system is hard, fear of annoying the shop, and no proof anyone pays. A pool has none of these. Its serialized units cycle through repair invoices, exchange credits and core returns. The same P/N and S/N can appear on two invoices from one shop within the warranty window, and nobody joins invoice lines by serial number. Beside that sit credit memos issued but never applied, core credits not netted, no-fault-found evaluation fees on in-warranty units, and turnaround guarantees never credited. Pool gross margins are thin, so recovering 1-3% of repair spend moves EBITDA. The warranty windows are short and full of exclusions, so recovery has to be systematic, with a claim filed for every eligible unit.
solution: Input is one vendor-ledger export plus the invoice PDFs, with no maintenance-system integration. An LLM extractor builds a serial-level table: P/N (including interchangeable P/Ns), S/N, repair date, charges and the warranty text printed on the invoice or PO. Recovery runs in three passes, ordered from least to most disputed. Pass 1 is zero-dispute money: open and unapplied credit memos, duplicate payments, and core credits not applied. Pass 2 is the repeat-serial detector: the same S/N back to the same shop inside its window, plus the same S/N failing after different shops' repairs. Pass 3 is contested items: NFF fees on in-warranty units and turnaround-guarantee credits. Claims go out on each vendor's own form. A vendor playbook library covers the top 60 shops: warranty terms, exclusions, contacts, average days to credit and past acceptance rate. We chase every claim to a posted credit or cash. Phase 2 adds read-only receiving and removal data from the customer's ERP to confirm failures the invoices alone can't show.
why_now: Reliable, cheap LLM extraction from messy repair-invoice PDFs and warranty fine print is what makes an AP-only audit viable. Before 2025 it needed offshore data-entry teams, which killed contingency margins. Aftermarket parts prices and repair turn times have also climbed since the 2022-23 supply squeeze (my assumption, unverified). That makes each exchange unit worth more, so pools tie up more capital in them and each unclaimed failure costs more.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 20% of cash and credits recovered, or 25% on contested pass-3 items, with a 12-month tail after the audit. The fee is due only when cash arrives or the credit is applied, not when the memo is issued. That solves the objection to paying cash on a credit the customer can only spend at that shop. There is no upfront cost and no minimum. Year 2 adds a $2-4k/month continuous-monitoring tier for pools with over $15M of spend. Anonymized vendor-acceptance and turn-time data is a later product.
non_obvious_insight: Sequence matters more than segment. Leading with credits the vendor has already conceded gives first cash in 3-4 weeks, with no dispute and no relationship risk. That builds the trust to file contested claims later. Every contested claim, won or lost, adds to the playbook library: per-shop acceptance rates, exclusion language and time to credit. That library is the cornered resource and process power a generalist cannot copy. The pool is also the freight-audit shipper of aviation: high invoice volume, many vendors, serial-tracked goods and no reason to protect any single vendor.
first_30_days: Build a target list of about 60 pools and Part 145 stations from public repair-station and trade-association directories. Send 40 direct outreach messages offering a free scan: they send 12 months of vendor ledger and invoices, and we return the dollars found within 10 business days. The only thing we ask for is permission to file. Hire a retired warranty or materials coordinator as a paid advisor for vendor quirks. Close 3 audits and deliver ranked claim lists. File pass-1 claims first and aim for the first credit memo by day 30. Set an explicit kill test: if the median first-pass yield is under 1% of repair spend across the first 5 files, stop or narrow the segment. Publish the aggregate finding, such as the share of eligible repeat repairs never claimed, as the lead magnet.
lineage: mutation of I0195 ('Contingency Recovery of Missed Rotable Repair Warranties'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ramco Aviation (MRO/ERP software, warranty management module). White space: Caveat: this verdict rests on thin evidence. The WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) after the first two lookups. Every further search was refused, and I did not work around that limit. I could only fetch vendor homepages directly. I found no dedicated contingency-fee warranty auditor for rotable repair claims. I also could not rule one out, because I could not run Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or 'startup + key terms' searches. Vendor pages I checked (Trax eMRO, Veryon/Rusada, Pentagon 2000, CAMP) showed no warranty-claims features on their homepages, but homepage silence is weak evidence. I could not check IFS Maintenix (HTTP 429). Gaps that look unserved: (1) an outsourced, success-fee service that reads unstructured repair-invoice PDFs and joins them to removal records. This is the cross-system join the idea describes. (2) Small and mid-size operators such as regionals, Part 135 fleets and air-ambulance operators, which sit below the large ERP buyers Ramco targets. (3) The adjacent leaks, meaning no-fault-found fees within warranty, unreturned core penalties and turnaround-time guarantee credits. None of the vendor pages I read mention these. Unverified risks from my own domain knowledge, not from research: power-by-the-hour and maintenance-service-plan contracts remove warranty exposure for many small fleets. Shop warranty terms are often short and carry exclusions. Getting AP and maintenance-system exports from a small operator is hard. The addressable market may be small. Someone should check all of these before building. | How this version avoids them: Ramco's warranty module is software that large operators run themselves, and I could not verify its claims. This is an outsourced, success-fee claims service for smaller buyers, which Ramco does not offer. The Trax, Veryon/Rusada, Pentagon 2000 and CAMP homepages showed no claims features, though that is weak evidence. Generalist AP recovery-audit firms exist (an unresearched risk to check). They run duplicate-payment and vendor-statement logic and cannot read repair invoices, match serial numbers or judge warranty eligibility. Targeting pools and stations sidesteps PBH shielding, sidesteps the maintenance-system integration problem, and reduces relationship fear.

competitors.name: Ramco Aviation (MRO/ERP software, warranty management module)
competitors.what_they_do: Full aircraft maintenance and materials ERP that lists 'Warranty Management' as a feature. Its FAQ claims customers 'achieve up to $6 million in savings on warranty claims'. The page names no customer, gives no detail on how vendor-repair warranty claims work, and I saw no contingency or done-for-you claim filing. This is the only competitor I could verify. It is software you run yourself, sold to large operators, not an outsourced success-fee auditor.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established enterprise vendor (part of Ramco Systems, listed in India). The claim is marketing copy and I could not verify it.

I0195.evidence_of_demand: Essentially none found. I could not run forum, RFP or regulation searches because the search budget was exhausted. The only indirect signal is Ramco's marketing claim of 'up to $6 million in savings on warranty claims' (https://www.ramco.com/aviation). It suggests warranty recovery is treated as a valued outcome. It is unattributed, so it is not proof that anyone pays for outsourced recovery. I found no evidence yet of operators paying contingency fees for this, of RFPs, or of forum complaints about unclaimed rotable warranties.
I0195.kill_reason: n/a. Nothing found so far justifies a kill, but the research was incomplete. Re-run the existence check with a restored search budget before committing. Priority searches: 'aircraft component warranty recovery services', 'airline warranty audit contingency', Crunchbase/YC/Product Hunt for aviation warranty startups, and operator complaints about unclaimed repair warranties.
I0195.sharper_angle: Start with a wedge that needs only the accounts-payable export, so you avoid the hardest data-access problem, which is integrating with each operator's maintenance system. Run a 'repeat-repair detector' on repair invoices. Flag any part number and serial number that comes back to the same shop within the warranty window, and flag no-fault-found evaluation fees, core-return penalties and late-turnaround credits on the same invoices. This works the way freight and telecom audit firms do: an AP file in, a claims list out, paid only on credits recovered. Sell it first to Part 145 shops and parts pools that buy many exchange units, and to lessors and asset managers who need warranty compliance across a portfolio. Regionals and EMS operators can come later. Add the maintenance-system removal data as a second phase to confirm failures the invoices alone cannot show. Position it as outsourced claim filing and vendor negotiation, which ERP warranty modules like Ramco's do not provide, and not as software.
